chunks: From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Aban, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding a man who pledged a house to another man, and it burned down or collapsed, he said: 'His wealth (the value of the pledge) is in the dust of the earth (i.e., lost/absorbed by the debtor).'

And he said regarding a man whose slave was pledged to him and became diseased (or) whose goods were pledged to him, and he did not sell the goods, nor did he take care of them, nor did he move them, so they deteriorated: 'Does his wealth decrease by that amount?' He said: 'No.'

key_terms.تُرْبَةِ الْأَرْضِ: dust of the earth (idiom for total loss/absorption)
key_terms.جُذِمَ: became diseased (specifically with scabies or similar)

ai.seo_question: Who bears the risk of loss for pledged property in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the risk allocation in pledge (*rahn*) by distinguishing between natural depreciation and creditor negligence. It establishes that while the debtor bears the risk of the asset's destruction (e.g., a house burning), the creditor is not penalized for failing to mitigate losses on movable goods like slaves or merchandise, ensuring the debt remains intact. This ruling underscores the principle that the pledge serves as security for the debt rather than transferring ownership risks entirely to the creditor.
